vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits with his hands folded in his lap, fingers interlaced so tightly the knuckles have gone white. He's a large man-broad-shouldered, the kind of physical presence that comes from decades of outdoor work-but in the therapist's office, he seems to be trying to make himself smaller. At forty-seven, his face carries the weathered texture of someone who's spent most of his adult life under the African sun, but his eyes hold something else: a watchfulness that doesn't quite fit a man whose job is to protect wildlife in a national park.

Seventeen years ago, Marcus was living in a different country, working as a conservation officer in a region that had begun to fracture. He was there for the work he loved-protecting endangered species, managing habitats, training local rangers. He was engaged then, and the future felt uncomplicated. He was good at his job. People respected him.

The conflict came suddenly, though in retrospect, the signs had been there. One morning, armed groups moved through the park. Marcus was with two colleagues near the northern boundary when they heard gunfire. What followed was chaos that his mind still struggles to organize into a coherent sequence. There was running. There was hiding in the brush while violence erupted around them. One of his colleagues was shot. Marcus held him while waiting for help that took hours to arrive. The man survived, but Marcus remembers the weight of him, the blood, the sounds he made.

The park was evacuated. Marcus left the country within weeks, arriving in his current posting through a transfer that felt like escape. That was twelve years ago.

Now, Marcus works in a different park on a different continent, and he's very good at his job. His supervisors praise his dedication. He arrives before dawn and stays late. He knows every trail, every waterhole, every animal movement pattern. He's meticulous in his reports. But his colleagues have stopped inviting him to the staff gatherings. They've noticed that he doesn't sleep much-he's often already working when they arrive in the morning. They've seen him startle violently at unexpected sounds, have watched him scan the treeline with an intensity that seems unrelated to wildlife management.

Marcus doesn't sleep well. When he does, he's back in that moment-the gunfire never quite sounds the same twice, which somehow makes it worse. He wakes gasping, his heart hammering, and he lies in the darkness of his small house waiting for the panic to subside enough that he can think. Some mornings, he sits on his porch for an hour before he can move. Other nights, he doesn't try to sleep at all.

He's stopped seeing the woman he was dating. He couldn't explain to her why sudden noises made him feel like he was dying, why he needed to know where all the exits were in any room, why he sometimes couldn't hear what she was saying because he was listening to something else-something from seventeen years ago that his body insists is still happening. She was patient for a while, but eventually, patience runs out.

The park is still his refuge. Out in the landscape, moving through the terrain he knows, Marcus feels something close to peace. But even that is changing. Recently, he's been having trouble concentrating on the work itself. His mind wanders. He's made small mistakes in his reports. And the isolation that once felt like safety is beginning to feel like something else entirely-a slow erosion of the person he remembers being before everything changed.
